summary: Test v3 personal-essay mode: plain vs skill with depth-interview notes, and v3 vs baseline on original notes

unsupported_X: For about a year, I answered the phone at my dad's shop with "Hi, shoe repair."
the lie I'd been telling into that phone for a year
I said she must drive for work, her heel resting by the pedal
But noticing is how I caught the lie I'd been telling into that phone for a year.
worst on hard sounds like "C."
judged.reasons:
Both essays come in under the limit (X 644 words, Y 640) and build almost entirely from the notes. They differ in structure and in accuracy.

X is better built. It opens on the phone substitution ("For about a year, I answered the phone at my dad's shop with 'Hi, shoe repair.'") and puts the lie list next to it right away. That lets the mid-essay insight land: "On the phone I'd been doing exactly what I did with the test: swapping the true thing for an easier thing." X then turns to reading other people with a clean pair of lines ("Other people are easier for me to read." / "My avó, Rosa, is harder."). It uses the depth answer about the heels and avó, which Y leaves out: "I want the heels and my grandmother to be the same skill: reading someone from the outside when they can't tell you. But I can't tell what avó is thinking." It holds back the three-try phone call for a late climax.

Y opens hard with the confession ("Before I forged my mom's signature, I practiced it about eight times on the back of a math worksheet."), but it then mostly walks through the notes in order. Its climax, the realization paragraph ("I've been doing the same thing with the phone that I did with the chemistry test"), lands in paragraph 7 of 9. After that the avó paragraph and the career paragraph trail off without linking back to the theme. Y also tells the talent instead of showing it: "I can tell how someone walks from the wear on their heels". It drops the driver anecdote, which is the best piece of evidence in the notes.

On accuracy, Y is clean. X adds things the notes don't support:
- It fixes the duration of the substitution at "for a year." The notes only say the dad noticed after a year, and that she never once used the name until last month.
- It has her working out "she must drive for work." The notes say "it turned out she drives for work," so she learned it rather than deduced it.
- Its closing line, "noticing is how I caught the lie," credits her habit of noticing. The notes say "I only noticed when you asked me this." That closing line is also a tidy, aphoristic bow, a common AI tell, and it partly cancels the open "I'm still not sure" line right before it.

On human feel, X has more engineered rhythm: clipped fragments ("A small one, and not on the list."), paired sentences, and the "secretly relieved" cliché. Y keeps the student's loose phrasing and hedges ("just kind of embarrassed it took three tries", "they're totally different things", "my friends say I smell like a cowboy's basement"). It also uses long, natural comma chains ("kept it up for three weeks, through a progress report that needed a parent signature, until my teacher, Mr. Oduya, emailed home") and ends unresolved on "I don't fully believe her yet." That reads more like a real 17-year-old.

Net: X is the stronger essay for an admissions reader, but it has small factual drifts and a constructed ending. Y is more faithful to the notes and more human in voice, but its arc is weaker and its second half sags.

judged.reasons:
Both essays take their raw material almost word for word from the notes. They differ in structure and in what they choose to leave out.

Y has the stronger structure. It opens on the phone dodge, "For about a year, I answered the phone at my dad's shop with 'Hi, shoe repair.'" It then weaves the lie list, the chemistry test and the realization together: "On the phone I'd been doing exactly what I did with the test: swapping the true thing for an easier thing." Most importantly, it keeps the deepest reflection in the notes, which X leaves out entirely: "I want the heels and my grandmother to be the same skill: reading someone from the outside when they can't tell you. But I can't tell what avó is thinking..." Its transitions also do real work. After the lie section, "Other people are easier for me to read" moves into the heel notebook, and "My avó, Rosa, is harder" turns it around. Holding the successful phone call until near the end gives the essay a payoff.

Y has two weaknesses. First, the last line ties things up too neatly and is not supported by the notes: "But noticing is how I caught the lie I'd been telling into that phone for a year." Second, "for about a year" mixes up when her dad noticed with how long the habit lasted.

X has the more striking first line: "Before I forged my mom's signature, I practiced it about eight times on the back of a math worksheet." It also keeps sensory texture that Y cuts: "The shop smells like Barge cement and leather dust, and so does my hoodie; my friends say I smell like a cowboy's basement." After that, X reads like the notes rearranged rather than an essay with a plan.

- **It packs in facts.** "Carvalho Shoe Service on Pleasant Street, open since 1994, and since last summer I'm allowed to do heels and half-soles..." reads like a résumé crammed into one sentence.
- **It tells instead of shows.** It says "I can tell how someone walks from the wear on their heels" but drops the driver anecdote that would prove it.
- **Its turning point has nothing after it.** "I've been doing the same thing with the phone that I did with the chemistry test" lands in the middle. The essay then jumps to "Tuesdays and Thursdays after school, my avó..." with no link to what came before, and the grandmother material never connects to the main theme.
- **It ends on a side thread.** The closing line is copied straight from the notes: "I don't fully believe her yet." That is honest and not tidied up, but it leaves the essay without an arc.

On human-likeness, X has some natural roughness ("I kind of wanted stuttering and aphasia to be connected, but they're totally different things"). But stitching the transcript together in order, and trying to fit every fact in, is itself a sign of a generated essay. Y makes choices a skilled writer would make: it cuts the smell detail, the year 1994 and the cowboy line, and it uses deliberate short sentences ("I used to correct her. Now I don't. She can't say my name yet. She can say 'sapato.'"). Its tidy closing callback is a mild AI-style tell, so Y wins on human-likeness only narrowly.

On accuracy, X is clean: I found nothing in it the notes don't support. Y has the duration error and the invented cause in its ending. Even after that penalty, Y is the better essay for an admissions reader, because its arc and insight are much stronger.

judged.reasons:
Both essays stay almost entirely within the notes and reuse the student's own phrases. The difference is structure and insight.

X mostly transcribes the notes in the order they appear, so the threads never connect. It opens with the heel skill ("I can tell how someone walks from the wear on their heels... entry 1 is my dad's work boots"), and that thread is never mentioned again. The paragraph breaks are abrupt: "I also keep a list on my phone..." and then "I hate the shop phone." X also leaves out the grandmother completely. The weakest line is "Someone asked me recently what I understand now that I didn't then, and that's when I noticed." It hands the coach's question to the reader and gives away that the insight came from an interview. X does have real strengths. The aside "(We don't.)" is a nice touch of voice.

It ends that scene on the right note: "That was the best part. It was nothing to him." It then threads the main insight through the essay. "Only recently did I realize 'Hi, shoe repair' was a lie" leads into the chemistry story, and then back: "'Hi, shoe repair' isn't on it. I planned it."). It also turns the list's word "noticing" into a hinge ("I am good at noticing.") that connects the heels to avó Rosa. Y keeps her self-doubt intact: "I don't know if that connection is real or if I just want it to be, the way I wanted stuttering and aphasia to be connected. They aren't." Small details give the grandmother section its feeling: "She can't say my name yet. She can say 'sapato.'"

Y has visible tells of its own. "I know something about lies." is a constructed hinge. The staccato one-line paragraphs feel engineered. The ending is a tidy inventory, "For now, I have a list of 212 small untruths, a notebook of 61 heels, and one phone call... That seems worth practicing.", which wraps things up more neatly than X's open ending. Y also adds a few small inferences (dad running the shop "since 1994," "For years").

Even so, Y is clearly the better essay for an admissions reader, with a coherent arc and a real insight. It also reads more like a skilled human shaped it, while X reads like assembled notes plus an interview artifact.

judged.reasons:
X is the better essay overall, and Y reads more like a teenager wrote it.

**Why X is better writing**
- **Opening and through-line.** X starts in the middle of the scene: "Last month a man called Carvalho Shoe Service to ask if we fix purses. We don't." It states the main insight early ("Only recently did I realize 'Hi, shoe repair' was a lie. A small one, but a lie."). Then it ties the phone and the chemistry test together: "swapping the true thing for an easier thing."
- **The grandmother.** X includes the strongest emotional material in the notes: "She can't say my name yet. She can say 'sapato.'" It is also honest about the link it wants to draw: "I don't know if that connection is real or if I just want it to be, the way I wanted stuttering and aphasia to be connected. They aren't." This explains why she wants to work on "how the brain gets words back."
- **Y leaves out avó Rosa entirely.** As a result, Y's speech-pathology paragraph ("I want to study speech-language pathology, or something about how the brain gets words back") comes out of nowhere. It also sits awkwardly between the stutter paragraph and the phone call.
- **Y's loose pieces.** Y's heels paragraph is vivid but never connects to anything, except faintly through the last word, "noticing." Y also exposes the coaching session: "Someone asked me recently what I understand now that I didn't then." A sharp reader will recognize that as the interview question.

**Why Y reads more human**
- **X's AI tells.** X has heavy signpost pivots ("I know something about lies." / "I am good at noticing."). It uses a lot of short, staccato lines ("It wasn't panic. I planned it." / "Now I don't." / "They aren't."). It also states the lie insight twice. It ends on an inventory of three items and a tidy closing line: "a list of 212 small untruths, a notebook of 61 heels, and one phone call... That seems worth practicing." That kind of ending is a typical AI pattern.
- **Y's teen voice and texture.** Y keeps the student's own phrasing: "my friends say I smell like a 'cowboy's basement'", "way more than her left", "I felt kind of embarrassed that it took three tries", "(We don't.)". It adds detail X skips: "Barge cement and leather dust", "the finishing machine", "I finished the class with a B+".
- **Y's ending.** Y ends unresolved instead of with a neat lesson: "Maybe it goes on the list, though I still can't tell whether the list makes me more honest or just better at noticing."
- **The cost.** Y's sentences sometimes copy the notes almost word for word ("she laughed at that part", "never said anything about it"). That makes it feel more like a transcription than a shaped essay.

**Facts and length**
- X has three small claims the notes don't support: that the dad has run the shop since 1994, the "For years" duration, and implying she worked out that the woman drives. Y stays within the notes.
- Both are under 650 words: X is 641 and Y is 608.

unsupported_X: Why "shoe" came before "Inês."
Why she sometimes calls me Lurdes, my aunt who died before I was born.
I'm meeting many for the first time

unsupported_Y: I read a lot now about aphasia and how a brain gets words back.
judged.reasons:
Y wins on both counts, but only narrowly on writing. Both texts use the same material (sapato, flashcards, agulha and telemóvel, the driver's heel, 61 entries, the stutter/aphasia wish), and both stay under 250 words (X 242, Y 245).

X fits the prompt better. It turns the topic into actual questions: "What I want to know is how a brain gets a word back. Why \"shoe\" came before \"Inês.\" Why she sometimes calls me Lurdes." "Why 'shoe' came before 'Inês'" is the most memorable line in either text. "I read people from the outside" also compresses the heel habit well. But that line is an inference: the notes only say she can say "sapato" and not her name yet, not that one came first. Treating Lurdes as a question she is curious about is also invented framing.

X loses ground through packaging. "That's what I want to study, through speech-language pathology or linguistics: how to understand what's happening with someone who can't tell you" is a colon-thesis that recasts the stated study interest. The notes give that interest as "how the brain gets words back," not this. The closing "I'd like to find out" ties up a doubt the notes leave open. The "Why... Why..." run is a familiar crafted cadence. X also leaves out the glosses, so "She beats me at \"agulha.\" I beat her at \"telemóvel.\"" partly loses its joke for a reader who doesn't know Portuguese. Its register is smoothed out too ("completely different," "ground lower").

Y keeps the student's voice: "I kind of wanted stuttering and aphasia to be connected, but they're totally different things," and "ground down way more than her left." It makes the sharper link explicitly: "I don't know if that's a real connection or one I just want, like the stutter and the aphasia." That ties two wished-for connections together, which X only implies. Y also ends without tying anything up: "She said some of the best ones stutter. I don't fully believe her yet." That pays off the earlier "I have a stutter" and gives the topic real personal stakes.

Y has weaknesses. It states its curiosity flatly ("I read a lot now about aphasia and how a brain gets words back"). Its third paragraph crams the heels and the whole connection argument into one block, much of it close to the depth-session notes word for word. The ending on Halvorsen pulls a little away from the idea itself toward career doubt. It never names the field outright, only implying it with "to be one."

On facts, Y is nearly clean. X has several small inferences and framings presented as fact. X is the better-built essay, but Y reads more like a real 17-year-old and avoids the tidy-thesis tells.

judged.reasons:
Y is the better answer to this prompt. X is the more human-sounding text. Both are under 250 words (X 245, Y 242), and neither invents a major fact.

Y names the intellectual question outright and builds toward it. It opens with "My grandmother can say \"sapato\" but not my name," turns to "What I want to know is how a brain gets a word back," and then gives its best line: "Why \"shoe\" came before \"Inês.\"" That line connects the shoe shop to the grandmother through the meaning of sapato, and an admissions reader would notice it. Y also uses the Lurdes detail ("Why she sometimes calls me Lurdes, my aunt who died before I was born"), which X leaves out, and it names the field of study: "That's what I want to study, through speech-language pathology or linguistics." The arc runs from hook to question, to evidence, to field, to honest doubt, and fits the 'why' in the prompt.

Y's weaknesses are mostly signs of polish. Lines like "She beats me at \"agulha.\" I beat her at \"telemóvel.\"" and the repeated "Why..." fragments feel built for effect. "I read people from the outside" reads like a thesis sentence. "I'd like to find out." closes too neatly and isn't in the notes. Y also drops the glosses for agulha and telemóvel, so a reader who doesn't know Portuguese misses the needle-versus-cell-phone joke.

X reads like a real 17-year-old talking: "I kind of wanted stuttering and aphasia to be connected, but they're totally different things," "ground down way more than her left," and the strong unresolved ending, "She said some of the best ones stutter. I don't fully believe her yet." Its callback, "like the stutter and the aphasia," is earned. But X is mostly a transcript of the notes. The curiosity itself appears only in passing ("how a brain gets words back"). The third paragraph is long and lumps the heel anecdote together with the connecting idea. The Halvorsen ending moves from intellectual curiosity to doubt about a career, so the 'why' is implied rather than argued.

In short, Y is the stronger supplement for an admissions reader, though it shows some signs of craft-by-template. X sounds more authentic but has a weaker shape and less insight.

Y is the better answer to this prompt. Its opening, "My grandmother, Rosa, can say \"sapato\" but not my name," compresses two facts into one strong hook, and the shoe word quietly sets up the heels section. Y also names the intellectual idea directly: "What pulls me in is figuring out what's going on with someone from the outside when they can't tell you." Its turn from the heels to her grandmother is cleanly compressed: "Heels are easy. My avó isn't." Y closes on real stakes: "some of the best speech therapists stutter. I don't fully believe her yet." judged.reasons:
Both are within the limit (X 248 words, Y 247) and draw on the same material: the grandmother, the aphasia and the stutter.

**Why X is the better writing.** X is better at answering the actual prompt, which asks about intellectual curiosity. It states the idea outright ("how does a brain find its words again?") and then sharpens it into a real research question built on a concrete detail: "Avó can't say my name yet, but she can say 'sapato,' shoe... Why does one word survive and another not?" Its arc is clean:
1. Flashcards.
2. The question.
3. The disappointing finding that the stutter and the aphasia aren't connected.
4. A refocus on Rosa.
5. Her career goal (speech-language pathology).
6. The phone call as payoff.

The closer, "the man waited. I'd like to be the one who waits," lands the stutter, the phone and the career goal in one line. X is also economical. It sets up "hard sounds like 'C'" early and trusts the reader to connect it to "'Carvalho Shoe Service' on the third try."

**Where X falls short.** It pays for that polish with coached/AI-ish beats: "That stung, then helped," "handed me a question I can't put down," and the paired lines "She beats me at 'agulha,' needle. I beat her at 'telemóvel,' cell phone." It also invents two things:
- an emotional turn: "I had to stop reading about myself and start reading about her"
- the claim that "sapato" is "a word I hear every Saturday at my dad's repair shop"

**Where Y falls short as writing.** Y reads mostly as a close copy of the notes: "It's funny, because she's relearning words I'm learning for the first time," "I kind of wanted... They're not; they're totally different things," "She said some of the best ones stutter. I don't fully believe her yet." Its second paragraph is overloaded. It runs from the stutter to the shop phone to the 'connected' wish, then to a stray Lurdes sentence ("Sometimes she calls me Lurdes... now I don't") that has nothing to do with what comes before or after it. Then it jumps to the name insight. The intellectual curiosity is only stated ("How does a brain get words back? I read a lot about aphasia now") and never developed. The essay ends on Ms. Halvorsen's borrowed line, not on any idea of its own.

**What Y does well.** Its single best move is the most original insight in either text: "What the stutter and the aphasia do have in common is my name... Rosa can say 'sapato' (shoe), but not 'Inês' yet." It also stays strictly faithful to the facts. It adds "Hi, shoe repair," Ms. Halvorsen and "Carvalho is my last name," which makes it more specific than X.

**Why Y reads as more human.** Y is clunky, unpolished and full of teen phrasing ("kind of," "totally," "It's funny"), with a run-on middle paragraph. It reads like a real 17-year-old's draft. X reads like a skilled but noticeably shaped, coached (possibly machine-assisted) piece: tidy paired sentences, a compressed "stung, then helped" turn and a crafted callback ending. On craft and fit to the prompt, X wins.
